title: Filter employees whose email domain is "gmail.com".
shortTitle: Filter employees whose email domain is "gmail.com"

s1_definition.profdef: This is a `filter` whose predicate inspects the domain portion of an email address, typically with `String.endsWith("@gmail.com")` or by splitting on the at sign and comparing the part after it. The stream keeps only elements whose email belongs to the target domain.

s1_definition.oneliner: Filter on `endsWith("@gmail.com")` to keep only the emails from that domain.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** This is a `filter` whose predicate inspects the domain portion of an email address, typically with `String.endsWith("@gmail.com")` or by splitting on the at sign and comparing the part after it. The stream keeps only elements whose email belongs to the target domain.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** The compliance officer at the National Bank of India says, "List every employee who registered a personal Gmail address, so we can remind them to use the official bank email." The clerk checks each address and keeps the ones ending in gmail.com. That domain check is the filter.

**One line to remember:** Filter on `endsWith("@gmail.com")` to keep only the emails from that domain.

sections.s2_technical:
The cleanest domain test is `String.endsWith(suffix)`, which returns true when the string finishes with the given characters. For Gmail you test `email.endsWith("@gmail.com")`. Including the at sign is important, because without it an address like `someone@notgmail.com` would wrongly match a plain `gmail.com` suffix.

An alternative is to split the address on the at sign with `email.split("@")` and compare index one, for example `parts.length == 2 && parts[1].equalsIgnoreCase("gmail.com")`. Splitting is more precise and lets you compare the domain case-insensitively with equalsIgnoreCase, since email domains are not case sensitive in practice.

As always with real data, guard against null and malformed addresses. A predicate like `e -> e.getEmail() != null && e.getEmail().toLowerCase().endsWith("@gmail.com")` first checks for null, then lower-cases to make the match case-insensitive, then tests the suffix. Short-circuiting means the null case never reaches the method call.

A senior nuance: for anything beyond a simple domain check — validating full email syntax — you would use a vetted library or a carefully reviewed regular expression rather than hand-rolling, because email validation is notoriously tricky and a bank must not silently reject valid addresses.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — The compliance team at the National Bank of India found that some employees registered personal Gmail addresses instead of the official bank domain for internal notifications, which is a policy and security concern. They want a list of everyone using a gmail.com address so they can send a reminder to switch. The HR directory holds emails of all kinds. We must extract just the Gmail users. This is exactly how filtering on an email domain works — each address is tested for ending in the Gmail domain and only those are kept.

The code defines an `Employee` with name and email. A `ComplianceService` exposes `gmailUsers(List<Employee>)` using a null-safe, case-insensitive suffix predicate. The runnable `Main` feeds mixed-domain addresses and logs the Gmail users.

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: Rajesh (rajesh@gmail.com), Priya (priya@nationalbank.co.in), Amit (AMIT@GMAIL.COM), Neha (neha@notgmail.com), Karan (null email).

Step 1: The stream opens over five employees.

Step 2: Rajesh enters. Email not null, lower-cased to rajesh@gmail.com, ends with @gmail.com — passes.

Step 3: Priya enters. Not null, lower-cased, ends with the bank domain, not @gmail.com — dropped.

Step 4: Amit enters. Not null, lower-cased to amit@gmail.com, ends with @gmail.com — passes. This shows the case-insensitive match working on an all-caps address.

Step 5: Neha enters. Not null, lower-cased to neha@notgmail.com. Because we test the full @gmail.com suffix with the at sign, notgmail.com does not match — dropped. This is why the at sign in the suffix matters.

Step 6: Karan enters. Email is null, so the first test fails and short-circuiting skips the method call — dropped safely.

Step 7: `collect` gathers Rajesh and Amit.

sections.s6_takeaway:
To filter by email domain, I use a predicate that checks the end of the address with the string method endsWith, testing for the full suffix including the at sign, so an address ending in at gmail dot com matches. The at sign in the suffix is essential, because without it an address at a domain like notgmail dot com would wrongly slip through as a match.

In my banking project at the National Bank of India this was a compliance scan. Some employees had registered personal Gmail addresses instead of the official bank domain, which is a security concern, so the compliance team wanted a list of everyone on gmail dot com to send a reminder. I streamed the directory and filtered on the domain suffix. Because email domains are not case sensitive in practice, I lower-cased the address before testing, so an all-capitals address still matches correctly.

A senior point I add is defensive handling and knowing the limits of the simple approach. Real data has null and malformed emails, so I put a null check first and rely on short-circuiting to avoid a null pointer exception. For a plain domain check the endsWith approach is perfect, but if the task had been to validate full email syntax I would reach for a vetted library or a carefully reviewed regular expression rather than hand-rolling it, because email validation is famously tricky and a bank must never silently reject a customer's valid address.
